title: What's the deal with controlled burns?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore controlled burns (prescribed burning): how Native Americans and early settlers used fire to manage ecosystems, how Northern and Southern attitudes toward fire diverged after the Civil War, how Herbert L. Stoddard's Bob White quail research pushed prescribed burning into wildlife management, the role of fire in giant sequoia reproduction (Richard Hartesveldt), the failed burning of southern California chaparral, climate change and the feedback loop with wildfire, the step-by-step method of conducting a controlled burn, and a listener mail segment about the Canadian flag illusion and a Rush/Raymond Scott "Powerhouse" song credit.
topics: how to conduct a controlled burn

segments.title: Opening banter and sponsor
segments.summary: Squarespace sponsor read, then banter about a Bond side tree listener mail, a shout-out to Aaron Sites' short story collection, and jokes about the band name Controlled Burn.

segments.title: Native American fire management and pre-Columbian ecosystems
segments.summary: Discussion of how archaeologists long underestimated Native American land management, including their use of fire to manage ecosystems for foraging, visibility and access, and how fire management was nearly universal.

segments.title: Settlement patterns and North-South attitudes toward fire
segments.summary: The hosts discuss an academic article on the historical foundations of prescribed burning, linking English settler origins in the Northeast and South to differing farming experience and fire attitudes, and how Northern landowners who bought Southern plantations stopped fire use.

segments.title: Herbert Stoddard and Bob White quail
segments.summary: Plantation owners including Henry Bedell hired the U.S. Bureau of Biological Survey, which brought in Herbert L. Stoddard after Bob White quail populations declined. Stoddard found woody undergrowth, caused by halted burning, was the problem and advocated fire, but was resisted for decades until the 1970s, with the U.S. Forest Service symposium in 1991 cited as a turning point.

segments.title: Fire benefits: fuel reduction, canopy and sequoia reproduction
segments.summary: Controlled burns reduce understory fuel to prevent wildfires, open the canopy, and aid reproduction. Giant sequoias in Yosemite need fire to open cones, as shown by Richard Hartesveldt's tests in the 1960s.

segments.title: Chaparral and climate change
segments.summary: Burning southern California chaparral failed to reduce wildfires and promoted more flammable growth. The hosts then discuss the wildfire-climate feedback loop, global fire season lengthening, and the Fort McMurray wildfire in Canada.

segments.title: How a controlled burn is conducted
segments.summary: Steps include permits and local authorities, choosing weather with damp conditions and low wind, planning natural and manufactured firebreaks, a test fire, then backfire, flank fires and head fire, followed by mop-up. Hosts also note that fire crews are generally experienced wildfire teams, and a warning not to attempt burns.
topics: how to conduct a controlled burn

segments.title: Listener mail: Canadian flag faces and Rush Powerhouse credit
segments.summary: A listener reports Josh humming Rush's Limelight-era piece instead of Raymond Scott's Powerhouse, and mentions the Canadian flag face illusion and Sister Wendy. Another listener adds that Rush settled a Powerhouse infringement via a one-time payment.
